title: What a Telegram bot is good for
metaTitle: Telegram bot for business, a short list
excerpt: A Telegram bot fits a known group and a short command list: status, intake, and alerts. It is a poor substitute for a product that should be a screen.

faqs.question: What is a Telegram bot good for in a business?
faqs.answer: Use it for a known group and a short list of commands, usually status, intake, and alerts. Each command reads a source you trust or writes a record a person will see. It is a poor home for a product people have not asked to use inside a chat.

faqs.question: Who should be allowed to run the commands?
faqs.answer: Start in a private chat or a private group. Decide who may ask for status, who may submit intake, and who may trigger an alert. A status command that reveals a customer's file to a public group is a leak. Widen a command only when that wider audience is safe.

faqs.question: What if someone asks a question the bot does not handle?
faqs.answer: Say that it does not know, and give a way to reach a person. The help text should list the real commands and that edge. An open chat that improvises answers will eventually send a confident wrong reply.

markdown:
A Telegram bot for business is a good fit when a known group already lives in Telegram and the jobs are a short list of commands. Status, intake, and alerts are the usual three. The bot is a thin interface over a workflow you can explain. It is a poor substitute for a product that people have not asked to use inside a chat.

If the group is not in Telegram, a bot will not move them there. If the job needs a canvas, a catalog, or a long record, a chat thread is the wrong room.

## What the short list is for

Status answers a question people already ask a person. Where is the order. Is the file ready. Did the payment land. The bot reads a source you trust and replies with the current fact, plus the time it was true. A status command that invents a narrative is worse than silence.

Intake collects a known set of fields. A name, a link, a budget range, a deadline. The bot asks one thing at a time, confirms the list, and writes it somewhere a person will see it. Intake is finished when the record exists. It is not finished when the bot has been charming.

Alerts push a fact the group would otherwise miss. A failed payment, a form that needs a human, a deploy that needs a look. An alert has a reason and a next step. A bot that posts every internal event will be muted, and then it cannot carry the one alert that mattered.

Keep the list short enough to fit in the help command without scrolling through a manual. If you need a twelfth command, you are building a product, and a product deserves a screen.

## A known group, not the open internet

Telegram works when the audience is already a group: a client team, a small community, a staff channel. People open the app for other reasons, and the bot meets them there. That convenience is the whole advantage.

The same convenience is a trap if strangers can command the bot. Decide who may ask for status, who may submit intake, and who may trigger an alert. A status command that reveals a customer's file to anyone in a public group is not an automation. It is a leak. Start in a private chat or a private group. Widen only when the command is safe to widen.

Write the help text in the brand's plain voice. Name each command, say what it needs, and say what it will do. People should not have to discover the interface by typing guesses. An example, labeled as an exercise: `/status` replies with the project name and the latest update. `/intake` asks for a link and a due date, then confirms both before saving. `/human` tells the person how to reach someone. Three lines of help are enough for that set.

## Where a bot should hand back to a person

Draw the edge in the help text, not only in your head. The bot handles the listed commands. Anything else gets a sentence that says it does not know, and a way to reach a person. Pretending to answer an open question is how a confident wrong reply gets forwarded to a customer.

Payments, deletions, and anything the person cannot undo should not be a bare command. If the group wants those later, the command can prepare a draft, and a person confirms it before anything is sent. The first version does not need them.

The W3C notes that the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) can also be applied to software, not only to web pages, under principles that include understandable and operable. A bot people must operate should make the available actions obvious and the replies plain. A command that fails should say what was missing. A reply that succeeds should say what was saved. Those two sentences are the interface.

## What to skip

Skip a bot that is supposed to replace the website, the inbox, and the product in one thread. Chat is a poor home for comparing options, reading a long policy, or learning a new tool. Link out to the page that already does that job. The bot can carry the link. It does not have to host the experience.

Skip open-ended conversation as a feature. A model that chats will be asked questions outside the three commands, and it will answer some of them badly. If you want a narrower assist, keep it inside a command with a template, and keep the source of the facts visible in the reply. "According to the project update from Tuesday" is a status. A paragraph with no source is a guess.

Skip building the bot before the manual version is boring. If the team does not already answer status by looking at one place, the bot has nothing reliable to read. Fix the source first. Then the command is a window on that source.

Give the bot an owner the way you would give a page an owner. Someone watches the first weeks of replies, updates the help text when a command changes, and turns a command off when the source behind it is no longer true. A bot without that person becomes a confident outdated notice. The group will learn to ignore it, and then a real alert has nowhere to land.

## A different room for a community

Telegram is one room. Some communities already talk somewhere else, and the bot should follow them rather than recruit them. If the group lives in Discord, the same idea, commands as a small interface, belongs there. That piece is [Discord bots as a product surface](/blog/discord-bots-as-a-product-surface).

The test for either room is the same. A new member can read the help text and complete one command without asking what the bot is for.

If a short command list is the right shape for a workflow you already run, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds that kind of bot when the group and the jobs are specific.
